question: A mid-sized online furniture retailer runs its storefront on GKE and currently accepts credit card numbers in its own checkout form, which sends the primary account number (PAN) through its API tier to a payment processor. The annual PCI DSS assessment is expensive because the entire platform is in scope. The CFO wants to cut the assessment scope as much as possible without redesigning the storefront. What should you recommend?
options: Move the checkout API to Cloud Run so that the serverless platform's PCI attestation covers the cardholder data environment.

Integrate the payment processor's hosted payment fields or redirect so that card data goes directly from the customer's browser to the processor, and store only the returned payment token in your systems.
Encrypt the PAN with a Cloud KMS key in the API tier before storing it in Cloud SQL, and rotate the key every 90 days.
Place the GKE cluster inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter so that cardholder data cannot be exfiltrated to other projects.
explanation: The most effective way to shrink PCI DSS scope is to keep cardholder data out of your environment entirely: with hosted fields or a redirect, the PAN travels straight from the browser to the PCI-certified processor and your systems only handle a non-sensitive token, so the storefront largely falls out of the cardholder data environment. Option A is wrong because using a compliant platform does not remove your application from scope if it still processes PANs; compliance is shared. Option C still stores PANs, which keeps the database, keys and surrounding systems in scope. Option D reduces exfiltration risk but does not change what data flows through your systems, so the scope stays the same.
hint: Core Rule (PCI DSS scope reduction): The most effective way to shrink PCI DSS scope is to keep cardholder data out of your environment entirely: with hosted fields or a redirect, the PAN travels straight from the browser to the PCI-certified processor and your systems only handle a non-sensitive token, so the storefront largely falls out of the cardholder data environment.

question: A payments startup is preparing for its first PCI DSS assessment of a cardholder data environment (CDE) built on Compute Engine and Cloud SQL. The Qualified Security Assessor has asked which controls the startup must evidence itself and which it can inherit from Google Cloud. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The startup must implement and evidence network segmentation of the CDE, for example with dedicated VPCs, firewall rules and Cloud NGFW policies.
Google Cloud's PCI DSS Attestation of Compliance means the startup's application inherits full PCI DSS compliance for the CDE.
The startup can download Google Cloud's PCI DSS Attestation of Compliance and responsibility matrix from Compliance Reports Manager to evidence inherited physical and infrastructure controls.
Google Cloud performs quarterly vulnerability scans of the startup's VM operating systems and application code as part of the platform attestation.
The startup must file its Report on Compliance with Google Cloud before deploying the CDE to production.
explanation: PCI DSS follows the shared responsibility model: Google's Attestation of Compliance and PCI responsibility matrix, available through Compliance Reports Manager, evidence the physical and infrastructure controls Google operates, while the customer must build and evidence its own controls such as CDE segmentation, patching, logging, vulnerability scanning and access management. Option B overstates inheritance; the platform attestation does not make a customer application compliant. Option D is wrong because scanning customer operating systems and code is the customer's responsibility (Security Command Center's web security scanner can help but the obligation is the customer's). Option E is not a real requirement; reports are filed with acquirers or card brands, not with Google.
hint: Core Rule (PCI DSS shared responsibility): PCI DSS follows the shared responsibility model: Google's Attestation of Compliance and PCI responsibility matrix, available through Compliance Reports Manager, evidence the physical and infrastructure controls Google operates, while the customer must build and evidence its own controls such as CDE segmentation, patching, logging, vulnerability scanning and access management.

question: A media conglomerate has more than 500 BigQuery datasets spread across 80 projects, created by different business units over several years. question: A telecom operator wants to give its data science team access to call detail records in BigQuery. The records include subscriber phone numbers, which must not be visible in clear text. The analysts need to join records for the same subscriber across several tables, downstream legacy tools validate that the field is exactly 10 digits, and the fraud team must be able to recover the original number for a specific record when a case is escalated. Which Sensitive Data Protection transformation should you use?
options: Format-preserving encryption (FPE-FFX) with a Cloud KMS-wrapped key and a numeric alphabet.
Cryptographic hashing with a Cloud KMS-wrapped key.
Replacement with the infoType name, for example PHONE_NUMBER.
Deterministic encryption (AES-SIV) with a surrogate annotation.
explanation: FPE-FFX is deterministic, so the same input always yields the same token and joins keep working; it preserves the length and character set of the input, so a 10-digit number remains a 10-digit number for the legacy validation; and it is reversible by an authorized caller holding the wrapped key, which satisfies the fraud team's re-identification need. Option B is deterministic but irreversible, so escalations could not recover the number. Option C destroys both uniqueness and reversibility. Option D is deterministic and reversible but produces a longer base64 surrogate that would fail the 10-digit format check.
hint: Core Rule (Format-preserving encryption): FPE-FFX is deterministic, so the same input always yields the same token and joins keep working; it preserves the length and character set of the input, so a 10-digit number remains a 10-digit number for the legacy validation; and it is reversible by an authorized caller holding the wrapped key, which satisfies the fraud team's re-identification need.

question: A loyalty program operator must give an external marketing analytics agency a dataset of purchase events. Option A is reversible, which the DPO prohibited for the recipient side and adds unnecessary risk. Option B is also reversible and makes the output look like a real email, which is undesirable. hint: Core Rule (Pseudonymization): A keyed cryptographic hash (HMAC) produces the same output for the same email, preserving per-customer analytics, and is one-way; because the key is wrapped in Cloud KMS and never given to the agency, they cannot rebuild the mapping even by hashing candidate emails.

question: A public health institute plans to publish a de-identified BigQuery dataset of hospital admissions to academic researchers. Direct identifiers have already been removed, but the dataset still contains ZIP code, birth date and gender. The privacy board is concerned that combinations of these fields could single out individuals and asks for a quantitative measure before release. What should you do?

Encrypt the ZIP code and birth date columns with a customer-managed encryption key in Cloud KMS before publishing.
explanation: The concern is re-identification through quasi-identifiers, which is measured with metrics such as k-anonymity; Sensitive Data Protection risk analysis computes k-anonymity (and l-diversity, k-map and delta-presence) over BigQuery tables so the institute can iteratively generalize fields until the dataset satisfies the board's threshold. Option A only looks for direct identifiers and gives false assurance about linkage attacks. Option C blocks the columns entirely, which defeats the research purpose and does not quantify risk. Option D protects data at rest but the published dataset would either be unusable or, once decrypted, just as re-identifiable.
hint: Core Rule (Re-identification risk analysis): The concern is re-identification through quasi-identifiers, which is measured with metrics such as k-anonymity; Sensitive Data Protection risk analysis computes k-anonymity (and l-diversity, k-map and delta-presence) over BigQuery tables so the institute can iteratively generalize fields until the dataset satisfies the board's threshold.

question: A credit union stores a member table in BigQuery with 40 columns, including social security number and date of birth. Marketing analysts need to query most of the table, but only the fraud team may read the two sensitive columns. You want to enforce this in a single table without maintaining copies and to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

Option D works but requires application-level key handling, changes every query, and is harder to audit than the built-in column-level security.
hint: Core Rule: Policy tags provide native BigQuery column-level security: once access control is enforced on the taxonomy, users without the Data Catalog Fine-Grained Reader role on the tag cannot query the tagged columns even though they have table-level access, so analysts can still use SELECT on the remaining columns.

question: A consumer goods company keeps all sales transactions in one large BigQuery table partitioned by date. question: A subscription-box company stores payment card numbers so it can charge customers monthly. question: A multinational bank has dozens of data-producing projects that each publish BigQuery tables. question: A retail analytics team maintains more than 150 curated views in a dataset named curated that read from a locked-down raw dataset containing customer PII. Every time an engineer adds a view, an administrator must authorize it on the raw dataset, which delays releases and has led to broken dashboards. You need to remove this friction while keeping consumers unable to read the raw tables directly. What should you do?
options: Grant the analytics team the BigQuery Data Viewer role on the raw dataset so that new views work immediately.

Authorize the entire curated dataset on the raw dataset (an authorized dataset) so that all current and future views in it can read the raw tables without individual authorization.
explanation: Authorized datasets extend the authorized view concept to a whole dataset: once curated is authorized on raw, any view created in curated can query raw tables, and consumers still only receive access to curated, so the per-view administrative step disappears without weakening the boundary. Option A gives the whole team direct access to PII, defeating the control. Option B duplicates data, adds cost and staleness, and the scheduled queries would themselves need access. Option C copies raw data into snapshots, which also exposes PII and does not address view authorization.
hint: Core Rule (BigQuery authorized datasets): Authorized datasets extend the authorized view concept to a whole dataset: once curated is authorized on raw, any view created in curated can query raw tables, and consumers still only receive access to curated, so the per-view administrative step disappears without weakening the boundary.

question: A bank configured BigQuery dynamic data masking on an account_number column using a policy tag with a masking rule. A fraud analyst who is in the group holding the Masked Reader role reports that she sees full account numbers rather than masked values, while her colleagues in the same group see masked values. Security asks you to explain and fix the discrepancy. What is the most likely cause and correction?
options: The masking rule was created after her session started; ask her to sign out and back in so the rule takes effect.
She also holds the Fine-Grained Reader role on the policy tag, directly or through another group, which takes precedence over Masked Reader; remove that grant if she should only see masked data.
Dynamic data masking only applies to queries from Looker Studio; her SQL workbench bypasses the rule, so she must be moved to Looker Studio.
The column has two masking rules and BigQuery picked the raw one; delete the second rule.
explanation: When a principal has both the Fine-Grained Reader and Masked Reader roles on the same policy tag, BigQuery grants full access and returns the raw value, so a user who inherits Fine-Grained Reader through another group will see unmasked data while peers with only Masked Reader see masked results; the fix is to remove the broader grant. Option A is wrong because masking is evaluated at query time, not per session. Option C is false: masking applies to all query paths including the API and SQL tools. Option D misdescribes how rules work; multiple rules are resolved by a documented precedence order, and none of them return raw data to a Masked Reader.
hint: Core Rule (Data masking precedence): When a principal has both the Fine-Grained Reader and Masked Reader roles on the same policy tag, BigQuery grants full access and returns the raw value, so a user who inherits Fine-Grained Reader through another group will see unmasked data while peers with only Masked Reader see masked results; the fix is to remove the broader grant.
